name: scoped-locking
intent: Bind a lock's lifetime to the lifetime of a scope so that the lock is acquired when control enters the scope and released automatically on every exit path, not merely on the path the programmer remembered.
problem: Critical sections that acquire and release a lock explicitly are correct only as long as every exit path releases it. A later early return, a newly thrown exception, a cancellation or a routine maintenance edit adds an exit path without an unlock, and the leaked lock blocks every subsequent thread forever.
context: Concurrent code that serializes shared mutable state with a mutex or similar synchronizer and whose guarded region has more than one exit path (early returns, exceptions, cancellation, callbacks). It applies wherever the language provides a reliable scope-exit hook - a destructor (RAII), try/finally, using, with, defer or a block-scoped synchronizer - or where one can be emulated without losing the guarantee.
benefits: Release is guaranteed on every exit path - normal return, early return, exception and block exit - eliminating the whole class of 'forgot to unlock' defects.
Acquire and release are written once, at the top of the critical section, instead of being duplicated at each exit; the language or runtime, not the programmer, enforces the pairing.
Critical sections become auditable at a glance: the guard's scope is the critical section, so lock coverage and lock duration can be reviewed by reading structure rather than tracing returns.

Substitutable locking strategies: a guard parameterized by the lock type lets one critical-section body run under a mutex, a recursive mutex, a readers-writer lock or a null lock (Strategized Locking).
Success and failure paths need no separate unlock discipline: error handling inside the scope does not have to know about the lock.
tradeoffs: The lock is held for the whole lexical scope, so logging, a blocking call or a refactor that moves work inside the braces silently lengthens the critical section and increases contention.
Recursive or nested acquisition self-deadlocks on a non-recursive mutex, and the guard hides the acquisition from readers of the body (the reason Thread-Safe Interface exists).

Non-local exits that bypass scope cleanup still skip the release: thread exit or cancellation inside the guarded region, or any environment where the scope-exit hook is a macro or a convention rather than a runtime guarantee.
Guard lifetime is not always visible at the call site: an unnamed temporary guard in C++ unlocks immediately, and a guard captured by a longer-lived closure releases far later than the code suggests.

Lock ordering is not addressed at all - two scoped locks taken in opposite orders still deadlock; deadlock avoidance has to be arranged separately, for example by a variadic multi-lock or a documented ordering.

The pattern makes it easy to hold a lock across blocking work: a scope spanning I/O, a condition wait or an await point blocks peers for its whole duration, and some languages reject the combination outright.

Shapes a plain guard cannot express: release-while-waiting for condition variables, lock upgrade/downgrade for readers-writer locks and try-lock or timed acquisition all need richer lock types or a different guard.

participants.responsibility: Object or language construct whose entry acquires the lock and whose exit releases it on every path, including exceptions; it owns the acquire/release pairing and nothing else.
The synchronizer (mutex, recursive mutex, readers-writer lock, semaphore) whose acquire and release operations the guard invokes.
The shared-state operation that must run under mutual exclusion; it contains no locking code of its own.
Executes the scope: declares the guard at the top of the critical section and never calls the lock's acquire or release operations directly.

use_cases: Incrementing a shared hit counter or metrics table from request threads (POSA2's canonical hit-count example), where the method has several bail-out paths.
Guarding an in-memory cache or registry around find-or-create, where the lookup may insert, miss, fail or throw.
Updating session or connection state under a per-object lock in a server that processes many concurrent connections (ACE's ACE_Guard on ACE_Thread_Mutex).
Multi-mutex operations such as a bank transfer, where std::scoped_lock or std::lock acquires both guards deadlock-free and releases them at scope exit.
Suspending critical sections in coroutine code (kotlinx.coroutines Mutex.withLock, tokio::sync::Mutex) where the guard must survive suspension points.
Logging and serialization subsystems that must not keep the lock if a formatter or sink throws.
Java synchronized blocks, C# lock statements, Python with statements and Ruby synchronize blocks around read-modify-write on shared collections.

Go's idiomatic scoped lock: mu.Lock() immediately followed by defer mu.Unlock() at the top of the function, so every return path and panic releases the mutex (Go sync.Mutex); note a Go mutex is not bound to the locking goroutine, so any goroutine may unlock it.

Rust std::sync::Mutex: Mutex::lock returns a MutexGuard whose Deref/DerefMut expose the data and whose Drop unlocks at end of scope; the guard is deliberately !Send so the release always happens on the acquiring thread.

Chromium's base::AutoLock family (AutoLock, AutoTryLock, AutoUnlock, ReleasableAutoLock) guarding members annotated for Clang thread-safety analysis, with copy operations deleted so the guard cannot be duplicated or escaped.
avoid_when: The state is thread-confined or immutable: Thread Confinement or immutable snapshots replace the lock scope entirely.
The operation is a single atomic read-modify-write on one word: atomics, Interlocked or compare-and-swap are simpler and faster than a mutex scope.
Readers dominate: a Read-Write Lock or copy-on-write keeps readers concurrent, whereas a plain scoped mutex serializes them.

Waiting for a condition is involved: Guarded Suspension / Monitor Object with a condition variable must release the lock while waiting, so the plain guard is the wrong tool (unique_lock + cv.wait instead).
Work between acquire and release blocks for a long time (I/O, network, human input): snapshot the state under the lock and act outside it rather than holding the scope.
The application is single-threaded: a lock scope adds cost and hides that fact - use a null lock or remove the locking.
The language already scopes the lock (C# lock, Java synchronized, Python with, Ruby synchronize): use that construct directly instead of hand-building a guard.
anti_patterns: Unnamed or discarded guard temporaries (`std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);`, a monitor entered and left in the same expression): code that looks synchronized but unlocks immediately.
Scoping the guard wider than the critical section - locking around I/O, sleeps, callbacks into unknown code or whole request handlers.
Manual lock()/unlock() pairs kept 'because the guard is ugly', re-introducing the missing-release defect the pattern exists to remove.
Relying on a recursive mutex to paper over intra-object re-acquisition instead of splitting interface and implementation methods.
Treating lock possession as synchronization signalling (assuming that holding the lock means a peer's work is finished) instead of using a condition variable or barrier.
Holding a scoped lock across an await, a thread hop or a thread exit, where the language forbids it (C# await inside lock), the runtime deadlocks, or cancellation bypasses the release.
design_principles: RAII / scope-bound resource management: acquisition is initialization and release is destruction, so the resource's lifetime equals the lexical lifetime of the scope.
Exception safety and fail-safe defaults: release must not depend on the programmer choosing a path.
Separation of concerns: the guard owns only acquire/release, the critical section owns only the shared-state operation.
Least privilege / minimal critical section: hold the lock only for the state operation and only over the state it protects.
Encapsulation of the locking protocol: callers declare a scope, not a lock protocol, so the lock type can change without touching critical sections.
best_practices: Declare exactly one guard per lock in the narrowest scope that still covers the operation; never call acquire/release by hand in the same function.
Keep the critical section free of I/O, blocking waits, callbacks into unknown code and awaits; snapshot what is needed and act outside the scope.

Use the language's own scope construct (RAII guard, using/with, defer, try/finally, block synchronizer) rather than emulating one; where emulation is unavoidable (C), funnel every exit through a single unlock site.
Document lock ordering, and acquire several mutexes only through a deadlock-avoiding multi-lock (std::scoped_lock, sorted addresses) under one guard.
Prefer a non-recursive lock plus a flat critical section; treat a need to re-acquire as a signal to split into interface and implementation methods (Thread-Safe Interface).
Parameterize the guard on the lock type when the locking policy must vary, so the same scope runs under mutex, readers-writer lock or null lock (Strategized Locking).
Exercise the failure paths around the critical section in tests: force the exception or early return and assert that a later acquisition succeeds.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (Wiley, 2000) - Scoped Locking, Synchronization Patterns chapter (Ch. 4).

Schmidt, Strategized Locking, Thread-safe Interface, and Scoped Locking: Patterns and Idioms for Simplifying Multi-threaded C++ Components, C++ Report 11(9), September 1999 - 'The Scoped Locking Idiom'.
